headline: Not yet. But the IMF now calls an AI correction a top global risk.
summary: The IMF's stability report on Tuesday 13 October named an AI-driven correction one of three salient global risks and counted $650B of debt in circular AI deals. Seoul's Kospi closed down 5.46%, but the S&P 500 held flat as US chip stocks fell a fifth day.

analysis: The Kospi closed Tuesday 13 October at 6,035.35, down 5.46%, with SK hynix off 10.09% and Samsung Electronics 7.39% as foreign investors sold a net 4.51 trillion won; the forward P/E hit a record low 4.54, which Daishin's Lee Kyoung-min said prices in a 35–51% earnings decline. [1] Wall Street absorbed it. By mid-afternoon the S&P 500 was flat at 7,805.51 and the Nasdaq down 0.13%, but the PHLX chip index lost 1.2% for a fifth straight fall, over 8% in the run, with Micron down 5.4% and Applied Materials 8%. [2]

The IMF's Global Financial Stability Report, out the same day, named an AI-driven correction one of three salient risks to financial conditions, beside a sharp rise in sovereign yields and a major cyberattack, while not predicting imminent collapse. It counts 14 circular deals since 2023 where hyperscalers put about $300 billion of equity into weaker AI firms, plus $650 billion of debt, for $1.4 trillion of future revenue; hyperscalers now issue 10% of global investment-grade bonds, from under 1% in 2024. [4][5][6]

Positioning is stretched. Bank of America's October survey found 37% of fund managers overweight tech, up from 30% and the most since August 2020, with semiconductors the most crowded trade and 45% expecting an AI bubble in 2027. [7] The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 5.22% ahead of CPI on Wednesday 14 October, and JPMorgan missed with earnings of $5.57 a share. [3] Why 78: the IMF has put numbers on circular AI debt and chips are on a fifth straight loss, but US indexes held, so the score edges up. [2][4]
